formula_text: $S = 3x \quad \text{where } S \text{ is the magic sum and } x \text{ is the middle element.}$ \\ $a_{\text{first}} + a_{\text{third}} = 2a_{\text{second}} \quad \text{for elements in an Arithmetic Progression (A.P.)}$ \\ $\begin{pmatrix} 6 & 1 & 8 \\ 7 & 5 & 3 \\ 2 & 9 & 4 \end{pmatrix} \quad \text{for } S=15$ \\ $\begin{pmatrix} 15 & 1 & 11 \\ 5 & 9 & 13 \\ 7 & 17 & 3 \end{pmatrix} \quad \text{for } S=27 \text{ with odd numbers}$
page_context: This page, titled 'CHAPTER I - MAGIC SQUARES', defines properties and methods for constructing 3x3 magic squares. It introduces terms such as 'average' (a), 'row/column sum' (S), 'middle row/column' (m), 'diagonal' (d), and 'whole sum' (W). Key principles discussed include the relationship between the magic sum and the center element ($S=3x$ or $x=a$), and the observation that numbers within rows, columns, and diagonals form arithmetic progressions (A.P.). Two examples of 3x3 magic squares are provided: one with a magic sum of 15, and another with a magic sum of 27 where all numbers are odd. It also hints at a formula for the middle element when S and d are unequal.

This page focuses on problems involving the construction and properties of numerical 'squares' (matrices) and 'oblongs' (rectangular matrices). It provides examples of 3x3 squares where specific row, column, and diagonal sums are given, along with a formula for a central element. It also introduces a 3x4 oblong with an algebraic relationship between its elements (A+C=2B+3D) and a numerical fill-in example. The problems generalize to 4x4 squares, suggesting an interest in properties of matrices with varying sum conditions, related to magic squares but allowing for non-uniform sums.

This page is dedicated to the construction of magic squares. It presents algebraic templates for 4x4 squares (Fig I and Fig II). For Fig II, specific conditions are given: A+D=B+C and P+S=Q+R. Two numerical examples of 4x4 magic squares are provided, both having a magic constant of 34. Additionally, an algebraic template for a 5x5 square is shown, followed by an 8x8 numerical square. While most rows of the 8x8 square sum to 260, one row sums to 266, suggesting it might be a specific type of magic square, a construction step, or contain a transcription error. The overall theme is the systematic generation and properties of magic squares.
